entry.title: Motion Sensor Magic
entry.content:
I recently did some experiments with 24GHz human presence sensors and MeshCore. You can buy these sensors cheaply from AliExpress (just search for ‘LD2410S’).

The Wiring

I am using the (now old) Heltec StickLite for these experiments as I have heaps lying around, and they’re more than adequate for the job, but you could use any board for this. (the code is easily adaptable to any of the boards supported by the MeshCore project, which is over 100 at present).

This is an old pager project from the Ripple days, so ignore the wiring for the buzzer and the push button (these are not needed for this experiment). You only need 4 wires from the LD2410S to the main board:

Sensor -> Main board

  • 3V3 -> any of the 3.3V power pins (see red wire)
  • GND -> any of the GND pins (see black wire)
  • OT1 -> Serial RX (see yellow wire)
  • RX -> Serial TX (see green wire)

You can optionally wire the OT2 pin of the sensor to a digital input pin on the main board, and this can be used as a ‘wake up’ interrupt, if you want to try a firmware that sleeps to save power.

The Code

For sensors, you have to get down and dirty with the dev tools. There are way too many different sensors and behaviours/features to cater for in one generic, all-purpose firmware, so you have to program the specifics yourself.

To make life easier, I wrote a ‘simple_sensor’ sketch for the MeshCore project many months ago, to serve as a template for such firmwares. To make your life even easier, I have published a fork of the MeshCore repo with this specific motion sensor all done for you. (how amazingly generous of me!)

Just clone this repo: https://github.com/ripplebiz/MeshCore-sensor-playground

Checkout the ‘dev’ branch, then open it up in Visual Studio Code with the PlatformIO extension installed.

The specific target environment is: Heltec_StickLite_Sensor

If you want to see the specific diffs/commits for this motion sensor code, just see this comparison: https://github.com/meshcore-dev/MeshCore/compare/dev…ripplebiz:MeshCore-sensor-playground:dev

So, this variant creates a custom MotionSensorManager class, which encapsulates all of the management of the LD2410S sensor. The querySensors() method shows that 3 telemetry values are collected:

bool MotionSensorManager::querySensors(uint8_t requester_permissions, CayenneLPP& telemetry) {
  telemetry.addSwitch(TELEM_CHANNEL_SELF, _armed ? 1 : 0);
  telemetry.addPresence(TELEM_CHANNEL_SELF, ld2410s.isMotionDetected() ? 1 : 0);
  telemetry.addDistance(TELEM_CHANNEL_SELF, ((float)ld2410s.getDistance()) / 100.0f );  // convert to meters
  return true;
}

So, when you query the telemetry from this node, there will be these plus the board’s battery voltage:

Alerts!

The example firmware also creates alerts when the sensor is ‘armed’ and the isMotionDetected() is true. This is in the /examples/simple_sensor/main.cpp module:

Trigger presence_alert, critical_batt;
TimeSeriesData  battery_data;

void onSensorDataRead() override {
  float batt_voltage = getVoltage(TELEM_CHANNEL_SELF);

  battery_data.recordData(getRTCClock(), batt_voltage);   // record battery
  alertIf(batt_voltage < 3.4f, critical_batt, HIGH_PRI_ALERT, "Battery is critical!");
  alertIf(sensors.isArmed() && sensors.isMotionDetected(), presence_alert, LOW_PRI_ALERT, "Motion detected!");
}

The alerts are managed by the underlying SensorMesh class, and it handles dispatching a MeshCore text DM message to all users who are in the ACL, and are registered for alerts (if you login with the admin password, you get this ACL permission automatically).

So, you will see the unread message counter (and alert sound, if configured):

As an extra touch, the Ripple firmware renders the Home grid cell with an orange border when the sensor is in the ‘armed’ state, so you can quickly see whether your sensors are currently armed. It also renders the last telemetry value in the cell (in this case, the distance value).

Arming and Disarming

The example firmware supports some additional CLI commands, namely arm and disarm. This is handled by the code in the main.cpp module here:

bool handleCustomCommand(uint32_t sender_timestamp, char* command, char* reply) override {
  if (strcmp(command, "disarm") == 0) {    // example 'custom' command handling
    sensors.setArmed(false);
    strcpy(reply, "OK - now disarmed");
    return true;   // handled
  }
  if (strcmp(command, "arm") == 0) {    // example 'custom' command handling
    sensors.setArmed(true);
    strcpy(reply, "OK - now armed");
    return true;   // handled
  }
  return false;  // not handled
}

Conclusion

This is quite a handy node type to have. I plan to put a bunch of these around my house, inside of weatherproof housings, with solar panels, so that I can get intruder alerts. There are many more customisations you can make, and with the open code, you can change it however you like.
entry.summary: I recently did some experiments with 24GHz human presence sensors and MeshCore. You can buy these sensors cheaply from AliExpress (just search for ‘LD2410S’).

entry.title: Ripple UI v12.3
entry.content:
The latest release of the Ripple UI firmwares has a number of fixes and improvements:

  • epaper devices (Pro/Max/T5) now support dithering of colour map tilesets
  • some crash bugs now fixed
  • Map tile downloads over WiFi
  • New devices (MeshPager X2, WIO Tracker L2 Pro)
  • GPS compass arrow
  • Some multi-byte path fixes (eg. adverts)
  • Ripple Network: End of life

ePaper Maps

The T-Deck Max/Pro and the T5 Pro firmwares now support switching map tile sets, between dedicated black & white (whatever is in the /tiles-bw fodler) and standard colour OSM tiles (in the /tiles folder)

The colour tiles are now dithered and work surprisingly well. The translation of the colours is not always ideal, so you can manually adjust a contrast threshold value used by the algorithm, by pressing ALT+1..9. Below is the same map view, but with contast: ALT+5, ALT+4, ALT+3

The new Display preferences screen has the option for switching the map tile set:

Crash Fixes

There were three separate bugs found, related to multi-byte paths, and rxlog (Diagnostics screen). The crashes were only very intermittent, but so far the v12.3 seems to be super solid.

Map Tile Download

There is now a dedicated WiFi config screen (from home Extra menu):

Then press ENTER to save changes. You will then be prompted to reboot the device to apply the changes. This is a little cumbersome, but it really pays off in terms of battery drain if the WiFi is off from the boot state.

After enabling the WiFi downloads, you should see the orange dot from the menu which indicates the connection is successful:

NOTE: For the epaper devices, the map tile download is only for the color tile set option!

With the tile download enabled, the map tiles are downloaded (and saved to SD card) on demand as you zoom/pan. Note, there is no bulk tile downloading supported at this time.

New devices

Two new devices are now supported:

  • Seeed MeshPager X2
  • Seeed WIO Tracker L2 Pro

GPS Compass

When the device is moving, there is now a blue direction arrow rendered. For the new devices (X2, L2, and M9) which have a digital compass, the arrow is rendered even when device is not moving, and updates as you rotate the device (device must be horizontal).

The digital compass also requires calibration, and there is a new home Extra menu: Calibrate Compass

Ripple Network Type

Ver 12.3 marks the beginning of deprecating the Ripple network profile type. It has long since been eclipsed by the MeshCore network, and this version now does not allow creating Ripple network profiles. In future releases, the profile type support will be removed completely, but for now it will still load existing Ripple profiles.

Download

The new firmwares are all available via the MeshCore Flasher.
entry.summary: The latest release of the Ripple UI firmwares has a number of fixes and improvements: epaper devices (Pro/Max/T5) now support dithering of colour map tilesets some crash bugs now fixed Map tile downloads over WiFi New devices (MeshPager X2, WIO Tracker L2 Pro) GPS compass arrow Some multi-byte path fixes (eg. adverts) Ripple Network: End of life

entry.title: Companion Repeat Mode with the Wio Tracker L1 Pro

link.title: Companion Repeat Mode with the Wio Tracker L1 Pro

entry.content:
When a hiking group spreads beyond direct radio range, a device between the two ends may be able to help relay messages. This guide shows how to enable Companion Repeat Mode on a Wio Tracker L1 Pro, check that forwarding works, and use the results from a three-device field test to plan a temporary deployment.

How Companion Repeat Mode Helps

On a hike, a group can spread out as some people move ahead and others fall behind. If the devices at the front and back can no longer exchange messages directly—and there’s no nearby repeater—how can the group stay connected?

MeshCore normally keeps Companion devices from forwarding packets. For certain off-grid situations, Companion Repeat Mode allows a device to take on a temporary relay role. We took three L1 Pro units into the field to see how that setup works—and what to consider before relying on it.

Wio Tracker L1 Pro combines a built-in 2,000 mAh battery, an OLED display, an antenna and a protective enclosure in one portable device. It can be carried in a pocket or attached to a backpack with a lanyard or hook. The display is useful for checking device status, while the integrated battery makes the L1 Pro practical for a multi-hour field test. See the Wio Tracker L1 Series overview for product details.

Enabling Companion Repeat Mode

For this setup, A and C are the two endpoints, and B is the device between them that will relay messages. To enable Repeat Mode on B, follow these steps:

  1. Put all participating devices on the same supported off-grid radio setting.

  2. Connect the MeshCore app to device B and open its radio settings.

  3. Enable Repeat Mode

  4. Save the setting and leave B powered on between A and C.

If the app warns that the selected frequency does not support Repeat Mode, choose a supported off-grid setting that is permitted for your location. MeshCore restricts Companion Repeat Mode to specific off-grid configurations to help prevent portable clients from adding unnecessary forwarding traffic to a public mesh.

In our setup, B continued to use Companion firmware; we enabled Repeat Mode through the app, without reflashing it as a dedicated repeater. After the setting was saved, the device handled forwarding itself.

What We Observed in the Field

We then tested this setup outdoors to see how the phone connection and relay placement affected message delivery. For the field test, all three devices ran the same Companion firmware version and used the radio settings described above. Before testing, they exchanged adverts and were added as contacts. We chose an off-grid setting supported by the app and firmware, and confirmed that the selected frequency was appropriate for the test location.

The straight-line distances were approximately 4 km from A to B and 4 km from B to C. In Tests 1–3, B remained at the same location, surrounded by trees.

For Test 4, A and C stayed in place while B moved roughly perpendicular to the A–C line to a higher, more open location. The A–B and B–C distances remained approximately unchanged.

We sent ten short messages from A to C in each round:

The results show that B continued forwarding messages after its phone was disconnected. Moving B to a higher, more open location increased delivery from 4/10 to 8/10, despite approximately unchanged distances. In this test, improving the relay’s position made a substantial difference to communication reliability.

Practical Tips for a Temporary Deployment

The field results highlight how much relay placement can matter. Before using this setup on a trip, check the following.

  1. Agree on the radio setting before you lose coverage. Every node in the group needs to use matching settings. Choose a supported off-grid configuration that is legal in your region, and test it before the trip.

  2. Put the relay where it can hear both sides. A device inside a backpack may be shielded by the wearer or surrounding materials. Try clipping B outside the pack, keeping its antenna upright, or placing it higher and stationary. Test changes one at a time so you can tell which placement helped.

  3. Track battery use. The L1 Pro has an integrated 2,000 mAh battery, but actual runtime depends on usage and conditions. Note the battery level before and after each test, and bring a power bank for longer outings. Do not assume that a companion device will match the endurance of a dedicated, power-optimized repeater.

When to Use a Dedicated Repeater

Companion Repeat Mode is useful when a hiking group, field team or temporary outdoor event needs a quick relay and no fixed repeater is available. It can also help teams map coverage before deciding where dedicated repeaters should be installed.

It is not a replacement for a well-positioned, continuously powered repeater. A portable node can move, lose battery or leave the route where other users need it. For a fixed coverage area or long-term public mesh, use infrastructure designed for that role. The L1 Pro can stay in your pocket as a Companion during normal use—and become a temporary relay when the group moves beyond existing MeshCore coverage.
entry.summary: When a hiking group spreads beyond direct radio range, a device between the two ends may be able to help relay messages. This guide shows how to enable Companion Repeat Mode on a Wio Tracker L1 Pro, check that forwarding works, and use the results from a three-device field test to plan a temporary deployment.

entry.title: Boost Your SenseCAP Solar P1 Signal

link.title: Boost Your SenseCAP Solar P1 Signal

entry.content:
The Solar Node P1-Pro is a powerful off-grid repeater solution that can usually meet all your needs for reliable LoRa mesh network coverage. You can also swap in antennas with the corresponding gain to further boost its performance.

This guide will walk you through, step by step on how to improve antenna performance and how to verify that your Solar Node P1-Pro is working properly.

How to improve results

The antenna that comes with the Solar Node P1-Pro is already specifically matched for the device. In our tests, it can reach around 9 km in an open environment with a clear line of sight.

Before replacing the antenna, there are several simpler ways to improve the actual communication range.

Choose a more open location

LoRa performs best when there are fewer obstacles between nodes. Buildings, hills, dense trees, and metal structures can all weaken the signal.

If possible, install the P1-Pro in an open area and avoid placing it behind walls, inside metal enclosures, or very close to large metal objects.

Install the node higher

Installation height also has a large impact on coverage.

Mounting the P1-Pro on a rooftop, pole, balcony, or another elevated position can reduce obstruction from nearby buildings and terrain and give the antenna a clearer path to other nodes.

In some environments, simply moving the node a few meters higher can noticeably improve the link.

Keep a clear line of sight

For longer-distance links, try to keep the path between nodes as clear as possible.

A location may look close on the map, but hills, buildings, or dense vegetation between two nodes can still significantly reduce the usable distance.

When testing the maximum range, it is better to start with two locations that have good line of sight.

Pay attention to antenna placement

Keep the antenna vertical during normal deployment, especially when the antennas on the other nodes are also vertically polarized.

Avoid placing the antenna directly against metal surfaces or very close to large metal structures.

Sometimes even a small change in mounting position can improve the signal.

Upgrade the antenna for additional coverage

If the deployment position has already been optimized and you still want to improve coverage further, then upgrading the antenna is the next option.

A fiberglass antenna with suitable gain can provide better performance for fixed outdoor repeater deployments. In this case, you will also need to change the antenna connection to N-type and protect the exposed RF cable for long-term outdoor use.

Prepare in advance

  • Cable harness sheath or UV protective tubing, used to protect external SMA cables.

  • RP-SMA to N-type adapter, used for connecting high-performance antennas.

  • 868-915 MHz fiberglass antenna

Hardware upgrade

Install as shown in the picture

The included bracket also has corresponding mounting positions for the fiberglass antenna.

When disassembling or handling SMA connectors, make sure to turn off the node power first. Also, check the connector orientation before applying force. When tightening the adapter, ensure the connector fits snugly. A loose RF connector can reduce performance.

The internal structure of the Solar Node P1-Pro

Update the Solar Node P1-Pro firmware

You can easily update the firmware using the MeshCore Flasher, and following the steps below:

  1. Connect the SenseCAP to your PC using the USB-C port.
  2. Open the MeshCore Flasher website and select the SenseCAP Solar SenseCAP device entry.
  3. Enter DFU mode and mount the device as a removable drive.
  4. Choose the latest MeshCore firmware version and flash it.
  5. After the firmware update is done, connect to the device via USB and use config.meshcore.io to set up the location, radio region, admin/guest passwords, and power settings.

NOTE: Flashing the repeater firmware will disable the Bluetooth function on the node. MeshCore repeaters can be configured via a USB connection on config.meshcore.io or via the remote management tool in the MeshCore App. Please select the correct radio region (e.g., US/Canada 915 MHz) and set the transmit power and coding rate according to local regulations.

Pairing and managing with the MeshCore mobile app

After the repeater completes firmware updates and configuration, and the companion device has Bluetooth enabled, the companion device can discover the repeater through short-range broadcasting. This broadcast is sent when the repeater node powers on or when you press the user button.

You can log in to the app as a guest or an admin (if you set an admin password during USB setup). Guest access gives you telemetry data and basic tools. Admin access unlocks the command line and all settings.

MeshCore Repeater Transmission and Forwarding Verification

This method mainly checks three things:

  1. Can the repeater receive packets?

  2. Can the repeater send packets normally?

  3. Does the repeater actually forward data?

Check the basic settings

Connect the Repeater via USB serial port and execute:

ver
board
get radio
get tx
get repeat

Key point to check:

get repeat

Return:

on

At the same time, make sure the Frequency, Bandwidth, SF, and CR of the Repeater and Companion are completely the same. If the device supports it, you can also check:

get radio.rxgain

It is usually:

on

Test the Repeater RX

First, clear the stats:

clear stats
stats-radio
stats-packets

Then have the nearby Companion send 3–5 Channel messages in a row. Take another look:

stats-radio
stats-packets

Focus on:

recv
flood_rx
rx_air_secs
last_rssi
last_snr
recv_errors

If:

recv ↑
flood_rx ↑
rx_air_secs ↑

Indicates that the repeater has been properly receiving LoRa data. If these values don’t change at all after sending many packets, check the following first:

  • Radio parameters

  • Antenna

  • RX Gain

  • SX1262 / RF front end

Verify Repeater TX

Execute:

clear stats
advert.zerohop

Then check:

stats-radio
stats-packets

Normally, you should see:

sent ↑
tx_air_secs ↑

At the same time, nearby companions should be able to receive the repeater’s advertisement. If the stats show it’s been sent but nearby devices aren’t getting it at all, then focus on checking:

  • PA / FEM

  • RF Switch

  • Antenna

  • Transmission Frequency

  • TX Power

Check if the Repeater is actually forwarding

Enable Packet Log:

clear stats
log erase
log start

Then have Companion A send a few messages.

Execute after the test is completed:

log stop
log
stats-packets

Focus on whether the logs have:

RX ...
TX ...

If both RX and subsequent TX appear at the same time during the same test, it means the Repeater forwarded the data after receiving it. If you see:

RX ...
TX FAIL!

The reception is fine, but it fails during the sending stage.

Note:

RX quantity ≠ TX quantity

This is normal. MeshCore won’t resend every packet it receives; duplicate packets, hop limits, loop detection, and other conditions can prevent forwarding.

Recommended Test Commands

When actually checking, you can just run this set below:

ver
board
get radio
get tx
get repeat

clear stats
log erase
log start

stats-radio
stats-packets

Have the Companion send 3–5 packets, then:

stats-radio
stats-packets

log stop
log

Final test of active TX:

advert.zerohop
stats-radio
stats-packets

Final judgment criteria

The most important things to look at are these four points:

1. flood_rx / recv increases
2. RX appears in the log
3. TX appears in the log, and flood_tx / sent increases
4. The second Companion actually receives the message

If all four items are met, you can consider the repeater’s RX, TX, and forwarding functions to be working fine.

FAQ

Why can’t my P1-Pro reach 9 km?

The 9 km result was measured in an open environment with good line of sight. It should not be treated as a guaranteed communication distance.

Buildings, hills, trees, installation height, antenna position, interference, and even the location of the node can all affect the actual range.

If the range is much shorter than expected, we recommend testing again in an open area first before replacing any hardware.

Does installing the P1-Pro higher improve the range?

Usually, yes.

For long distance LoRa communication, reducing obstacles is very important. Installing the node on a rooftop, pole, hill, or other elevated location can often improve coverage significantly.

In many cases, changing the installation position can make a bigger difference than simply replacing the antenna.

Can I use a higher-gain antenna?

Yes, as long as the antenna supports the correct LoRa frequency band and uses the correct connector.

However, a higher antenna gain does not automatically mean a longer communication distance. Installation height, line of sight, cable loss, and the surrounding environment still matter.

Also make sure your final RF configuration complies with the transmit power and antenna regulations in your region.

Why did the signal become worse after replacing the antenna?

First check the antenna frequency, connector type, adapter, and RF cable.

A long or poor-quality coaxial cable can introduce additional loss. Loose connectors can also reduce RF performance.

If possible, compare the original antenna and the new antenna at exactly the same location and orientation.

Should the antenna be installed vertically?

For most normal deployments, yes.

If the other nodes also use vertically mounted antennas, keeping the P1-Pro antenna vertical usually gives more consistent results.

Avoid placing the antenna directly against metal surfaces or very close to large metal structures.

How can I quickly check whether the repeater is transmitting?

In MeshCore, you can manually use Send Advert.

This forces the Solar Node to transmit a LoRa packet. You should then see the corresponding TX LED flash briefly and other nearby MeshCore devices should be able to receive the advert.

The TX LED does not flash when another node sends a message. Is the repeater broken?

Not necessarily.

The TX LED only indicates that the Solar Node itself is transmitting LoRa data. It is not an RX indicator.

A MeshCore repeater also does not retransmit every packet it receives. If the Solar Node receives a packet but does not need to forward or reply to it, there will be no TX and therefore no TX LED flash.

So you should not use the TX LED alone to determine whether the repeater is working properly.

Why can the P1-Pro receive distant nodes but other nodes cannot hear it?

This usually means the uplink and downlink conditions are not the same.

First check the antenna and RF connector, then test with the original antenna in an open location. Also check whether the correct LoRa region is configured and whether the device is actually transmitting.

Testing two devices at a known distance and then gradually increasing the distance is usually easier than troubleshooting directly in a large mesh network.

Does adding another repeater always improve coverage?

Not always.

A repeater is most useful when it is placed somewhere that can communicate well with both sides of the network.

Adding another repeater in a poor location may not improve the link very much. In most cases, one well-positioned repeater on a high and open location is more useful than several repeaters placed behind buildings or terrain.

Can I install the P1-Pro inside a box?

The P1-Pro itself is designed for outdoor deployment, so normally there is no need to place the whole unit inside another enclosure.

If you do use an additional enclosure, avoid metal enclosures around the LoRa antenna. Metal can significantly affect RF performance.

If an external antenna is used, place the antenna outside the enclosure.

Purchase Links

  • Solar Node P1-Pro
  • RP-SMA to N-type adapter
  • 868-915 MHz fiberglass antenna

entry.title: Release v1.18.0
entry.content:
Download

Latest firmwares are in the flasher.meshcore.io

Change Log

New Features

  • #3298 Companion CLI (incl. new TXT_TYPE_CLI_COMMAND (3))
  • #3279 Companion: Node Discover UI
  • #3329 Companion CLI: new ‘get/set tz.offset’ command
  • #3357 WiFi companion CLI work. (new wifi.enabled/wifi.status CLI commands, etc)
  • #3442 Companion CLI: reboot, poweroff and shutdown commands added
  • #3458 Companion CLI: ‘get wifi.pwd’ added
  • #3402 Sensor node, telemetry push (subscribe/unsubscribe)
  • #3497 Companion: support for telemetry push

Enhancements

  • #3268 Add support for RAK12500 and RAK12501 GPS on RAK3401
  • #3249 Companion channel sync now faster
  • #3250 T114: Companion UI charging indicator
  • #3239 Repeater, loop-detect minimal now default
  • #3371 T-Beam-1W thermal fan control
  • #3459 Thinkode m7: BLE variant now has WiFi support
  • #3200 New ‘gps diag’ command
  • #3201 L76K GPS enhancements
  • #3202 Thinknode M6: xpose external-power and charger state (via ‘power’ command)
  • #3525 Meshtracker X1 & t100: GPS wake/sleep now faster
  • #3538 ‘hidden repeater’, now not discoverable if adverts turned off

New device support

  • #3180 Thinknode M8 support
  • #3248 WIO Tracker L1 1W support
  • #3108 Add Muzi Base board support (Duo + Uno + SuperIO)
  • #3463 Thinknode M4
  • #3574 Waveshare ESP32-S3 LR1121

Bug fixes and Other

  • #3275 Fix PA on RAK3401 when GPS missing
  • #3290 WIO tracker L1: Hibernate menu removed
  • #3234 Bosch sensor alt I2C address support (BME680, BME280)
  • #3236 Xiao C3 BLE companion fix
  • #3235 Companion CMD_SEND_RAW_DATA multi-byte path fix
  • #3218 LR2021 driver setTxPower fix
  • #3319 Fix Meshnology W12 TX power
  • #3379 LR2021 startReceive() fix
  • #3386 group channel data bounds check fix
  • #3395 Command buffer bounds checking fixes
  • #3389 ‘set af’ range check validation
  • #3002 nRF52 power management config fixes
  • #3393 extra null and range checks in packet pool manager
  • #3430 Thinknode M7 companion ethernet variant
  • #3449 Keep LED off before poweroff
  • #3431 Companion AbstractUITask overhaul
  • #3436 WIO E5 fixes
  • #3468 Thinknode m4: don’t touch crystal and OTA name
  • #3469 ‘set agc.reset.interval’ validation fixes
  • #3464 LR1121 DC-DC & Misc Updates
  • #3490 Heltec CT62 fixes
  • #1809 MACThenDecrypt, reject if not block aligned
  • #1896 preserve system time across reboots
  • #2472 T-Echo Lite: KISS USB variant
  • #3155 Promicro, added INA226 support
  • #3301 Fix clock on Heltec T1
  • #2065 T1000-E sensor power pin mapping fix
  • #2838 GPS: poll up to 5s for cold-start detection
  • #3568 tranport-code 0 now treated same as un-scoped
  • #3573 ACK direct-mode forwarding now applies retransmit delay config (was 0)
  • #2377 Low voltage boot lockout now disabled on most nRF52 boards

Companion CLI

With v1.18.0 of the MeshCore companion firmware, we have introduced a new Companion CLI.

This is similar to the existing Remote Management CLI that you may be used to using with repeaters.

Prior to v1.18.0 firmware, any custom commands that users wanted to add to companion firmware, would have to be allocated a new companion protocol command ID, and avoid conflict with other custom firmwares.

This was becoming cumbersome as new hardware variants released by manufacturers were starting to need custom commands to turn specific hardware features on and off.

Unfortunately this also meant companion applications would need updating to support the new custom functionality.

To make things easier, the new Companion CLI allows for a simple, text based, extensible command line experience for your companion nodes.

The companion applications no longer need to be updated when a new CLI command is added to the firmware.

As of MeshCore App v1.50.0, you’ll see a new Command Line option in the settings screen.

From here, you can send CLI commands to your local companion device. Any custom commands you may decide to register in the new handleCommand function of the MainBoard class in custom firmware will also be available.

Along with this, we have also introduced Remote Management of Companion nodes. A new Remote CLI permission has been added to the contacts database, and when this is switched on, it will allow that contact to send CLI commands to your companion node.

This is a very sensitive permission to grant, as it allows for managing radio settings, updating node names and also rebooting the device via the mesh.

A new Command Line button has also been added to the Contact Details screen in the Extra Tools section. This allows you to send CLI commands to other companions nodes via the mesh. You will only receive a response from the remote companion node if they have given your node permission to send Remote CLI commands.

We hope the new Companion CLI feature improves your experience in developing awesome things on top of MeshCore!

Multi Interface Companion Firmwares (BLE+WIFI)

Since the beginning, we have strived to keep our firmware sizes as minimal as possible, to allow MeshCore to run on the most constrained hardware available. To allow for this, companion firmwares have always been separated into individual BLE, USB and WiFi builds.

This helped to keep RAM and flash usage low, however it came with the downside of needing to reflash your companion node with a different firmware every time you wanted to change the connection method.

As of MeshCore firmware v1.17.0 in PR #3049, we introduced a new MultiSerialInterface class, that allows the MeshCore companion firmware to accept connections from multiple modes, such as BLE and WiFi at the same time.

This increases RAM and flash usage, however it allows users to connect to a MeshCore companion node via either connection option as needed, without requiring the user to change the firmware on their node each time.

When this was introduced, the only hardware board that it was enabled for was the Elecrow ThinkNode M7, which allows connecting via BLE, WiFi and Ethernet all from the one firmware.

With MeshCore companion firmware v1.18.0, we have expanded this to a few extra devices:

  • Heltec v3
  • Heltec v4
  • Heltec v4 r8
  • Heltec Wireless Paper
  • RAK3112
  • Xiao S3
  • Xiao S3 WIO

Users with these boards will now be able to connect via BLE and configure their WiFi credentials via the MeshCore App.

Some hardware doesn’t have enough RAM to allow for the coexistence of BLE and WiFi, and so these devices will still require you to choose from the specific connection mode firmware builds.

We are looking at alternative options, such as switching from Bluedroid to NimBLE for our Bluetooth stack, which drops RAM usage significantly, and can allow for BLE and WiFi on some of the more resource constrained devices.

For those of you who want to build your own custom firmware with BLE and WiFi support, for an ESP32 device that we haven’t enabled it for yet, all you need to do is add -D ENABLE_WIFI_INTERFACE to the build_flags and +<helpers/wifi/*.cpp> to the build_src_filter in an existing BLE variant. Please see PR #3591 for an example of how to do this.

The USB connection method is not included with the BLE+WIFI builds at this time, as it is used for serial logging. We will look to revise this in a future firmware update.

WiFi Settings in the MeshCore App

Now that we are starting to support BLE and WiFi at the same time, it makes sense to be able to configure it through the app.

As of MeshCore App v1.50.0 there is a new WiFi Settings section.

This will allow you to connect to your companion node via BLE, configure your WiFi credentials and when your node reboots it will automatically connect to WiFi.

For those using other companion apps, the WiFi credentials can be configured via the new set wifi.ssid and set wifi.pwd CLI commands.

Please see PR #3357 and PR #3458 for more info on these changes.

We hope these changes lead to a more enjoyable user experience, and we hope to roll these out to more boards in the future!

entry.title: Sensor Node Intro
entry.content:
The MeshCore sensor node type is much harder to get going with as we don’t pre-build variants with each release, like we do with repeater, companion and room server, so it requires some developer knowledge.

The reason behind this is because there simply are too many customisations that typically would be required to accommodate, and there would have to be thousands of variants. So, sensor nodes need to be designed for whatever purpose they’re intended for (eg. monitoring water level in a water tank)

Setup

You will need to install VSCode and once that is installed, within VSCode install the PlatformIO extension.

Then use Git to clone the MeshCore firmware repo:

git clone https://github.com/meshcore-dev/MeshCore.git

Starting with the example

The sensor firmware is essentially a starter or ‘template’ firmware, which has most of the components you’re going to need. In the project tree, it is in:

/examples/simple_sensor

Typical customisations should only need to touch the main.cpp module. This has a section which defines a MyMesh class, and this inherits from SensorMesh which provides all the plumbing and hooks which you can utilise.

Choose a board variant

A lot of the boards supported should already have a PlatformIO target env defined for the simple_sensor example firmware, like [env:Heltec_v3_sensor]. But, you may need to add your own env definition in a platformio.ini file in one of the /variant folders.

This sets up the build rules/dependencies, etc for that board+firmware role. You may need to modify the target.h/cpp files of the variant. These target modules assemble various global objects, like this:

EnvironmentSensorManager sensors;

This one is a kind of Swiss Army knife helper class which the other firmwares also use (eg. repeater) for doing the low-level work of managing physical sensors, like BME180’s, etc. So, most of that is done for you, but you typically have to ENABLE which modules your node is expecting to use. These can be enabled in your /variant platformio.ini file like this:

build_flags =
  -D ENV_INCLUDE_GPS=1
  -D ENV_INCLUDE_AHTX0=1
  -D ENV_INCLUDE_BME280=1
  -D ENV_INCLUDE_BMP280=1
  -D ENV_INCLUDE_SHTC3=1
  -D ENV_INCLUDE_SHT4X=1
  -D ENV_INCLUDE_LPS22HB=1
  -D ENV_INCLUDE_INA3221=1
  -D ENV_INCLUDE_INA219=1
  -D ENV_INCLUDE_INA226=1
  -D ENV_INCLUDE_INA260=1
  -D ENV_INCLUDE_MLX90614=1
  -D ENV_INCLUDE_VL53L0X=1
  -D ENV_INCLUDE_BME680=1
  -D ENV_INCLUDE_BMP085=1

Basic concepts

The sensor node can utilise these features:

  • Alerts (with High or Low priority)
  • Telemetry queries (ie. other nodes can pull telemetry from this node)
  • Time series data
  • Custom CLI command logic (eg. ‘turn switch A on’)
  • Telemetry push subscriptions (NEW: will be supported soon)

Alerts

In the example this is demonstrated with the Trigger class and alertIf() calls:

  Trigger low_batt, critical_batt;

  void onSensorDataRead() override {
    float batt_voltage = getVoltage(TELEM_CHANNEL_SELF);

    alertIf(batt_voltage < 3.4f, critical_batt, HIGH_PRI_ALERT, "Battery is critical!");
    alertIf(batt_voltage < 3.6f, low_batt, LOW_PRI_ALERT, "Battery is low");
  }

High priority alerts will re-try sending to nodes in the ACL which have the PERM_RECV_ALERTS_HI bit set. The sensor nodes will wait for an ACK, like any other text message.

Low priority alerts only fire off the message once and don’t wait for an ACK. These are sent to nodes in ACL with the PERM_RECV_ALERTS_LO bit set.

Telemetry

This is basically automatic as it’s a core mechanism in MeshCore. The target/variant sensor object will handle LPP encoding all the collected telemetry readings.

Normally, other nodes to need to request telemetry from your sensor node, and a telemetry response is then sent, but very soon you will also be able to subscribe to Telemetry push, where the sensor node sends telemetry packets to subscriber(s) but only when certain values change by some minimum amount. eg. a subscriber can send SUBSCRIBE request, and specify that temperature must change by 2 Celcius.

Telemetry push will have some guard rails to hopefully minimise abuse:

  • subscription has a timeout (returned in the subscribe response), so subscribers will need to re-subscribe.
  • must use a region scope (as fallback, if direct path is not established)
  • subscriber must specify which LPP channels/types and min deltas that these must change by to trigger push

Time series data

The sensor can collect periodic readings, and stores these (in volatile memory, in a circular buffer) using the TimeSeriesData helper class. Example:

  TimeSeriesData  battery_data;

  MyMesh(mesh::MainBoard& board, mesh::Radio& radio, mesh::MillisecondClock& ms, mesh::RNG& rng, mesh::RTCClock& rtc, mesh::MeshTables& tables)
     : SensorMesh(board, radio, ms, rng, rtc, tables), 
       battery_data(12*24, 5*60)    // 24 hours worth of battery data, every 5 minutes
  {
  }

  void onSensorDataRead() override {
    float batt_voltage = getVoltage(TELEM_CHANNEL_SELF);

    battery_data.recordData(getRTCClock(), batt_voltage);   // record battery
  }

  int querySeriesData(uint32_t start_secs_ago, uint32_t end_secs_ago, MinMaxAvg dest[], int max_num) override {
    battery_data.calcMinMaxAvg(getRTCClock(), start_secs_ago, end_secs_ago, &dest[0], TELEM_CHANNEL_SELF, LPP_VOLTAGE);
    return 1;
  }

Remote nodes can then send ‘min/max/average’ queries to the sensor node, specifying a time range. To achieve this, the querySeriesData() method must be overridden as above. The return value is the number of data series supported by this node.

Custom CLI Commands

Remote nodes can also enable actuators of different types, like turning an LED on/off, moving a servo, etc. by adding custom CLI command logic. This is done in the handleCustomCommand() method:

  bool handleCustomCommand(uint32_t sender_timestamp, char* command, char* reply) override {
    if (strcmp(command, "magic") == 0) {    // example 'custom' command handling
      strcpy(reply, "**Magic now done**");
      return true;   // handled
    }
    return false;  // not handled
  }

This should be fairly straight-forward to adapt to whatever your sensor node wants to do. Just return true to indicate the command was intercepted and handled, and place the CLI response in the reply buffer (which is sent to command sender node).

entry.title: The KISS Modem
entry.content:
What the KISS Modem firmware role is, what it isn’t, and who it’s for.

Since v1.16.0 the flasher has had a KISS Modem role for most boards (the role picker calls it “KISS Radio Modem”), and going by the questions on Discord the name confuses people. So, a quick rundown.

It’s the same MeshCore firmware and the same radio underneath. What changes is how you talk to the board: instead of the app, you open a serial port and speak KISS, an old and very simple protocol that amateur radio packet modems (TNCs) have used for decades. The radio stays on the board. Everything that decides what to send, and what to do with whatever comes back, runs on the computer at the other end of the cable. What you end up with is closer to a LoRa dongle for MeshCore than a node in its own right.

Who it’s for

Most people don’t need it. If you want to message from your phone, companion firmware plus the app is where to start.

The KISS Modem is for people building gateways or services on a proper computer. OpenHop (formerly pyMC) is the obvious example and can use a KISS Modem as its radio.

It doesn’t have to be a proper computer though. I have a Commodore 64 chatting on the mesh through one, over the user port at 600 baud, which is about all the stock KERNAL serial routines can keep up with. The C64 builds the packets and draws the screen, the modem does the LoRa and the AES.

It’s also handy if you want to poke at MeshCore packets from a laptop in whatever language you like, without flashing custom firmware for every idea. (The companion firmware can hand you raw packets too, and since 1.16 send them, but here you get the whole radio with nothing in the way.)

What is KISS?

Keep It Simple, Stupid. It’s the framing amateur packet radio has used between a computer and a TNC since the 80s. MeshCore didn’t invent it, it borrowed it because it’s simple and there are libraries for it in every language.

The way I think of it: KISS is the envelope, the MeshCore packet is the letter inside.

A C0 byte on each end, a type byte, and the packet in between. That’s why the protocol doc says any KISS client (Direwolf, APRSdroid and so on) can drive the modem: they’ll happily push raw frames out through the radio. It doesn’t get them onto the mesh though. They can open the envelope, but what’s inside means nothing to them, and the mesh won’t make anything of what they send either.

On top of plain KISS the firmware adds the MeshCore extras (radio settings, signal reports, battery, crypto) through a standard KISS command that plain clients ignore.

What the board does

Quite a lot, it just doesn’t do any of the mesh logic. It sends and receives raw MeshCore packets over LoRa. Received packets come up the serial link exactly as they came off the air, each with a signal report (RSSI and SNR) attached, and your software decides what to do with them.

The host sets the radio up: frequency, bandwidth, spreading factor, coding rate and transmit power. You can also ask the board for its battery voltage, the noise floor, packet counters and whatever sensors it has, and it can estimate how long a packet would take on air at the current settings. The protocol doc has the full list.

None of the radio settings survive a reboot. Apart from the board’s key pair nothing is saved, so your software sets the radio up each time it connects.

It listens before it transmits so it won’t talk over other traffic, and it takes one packet at a time: it tells you when a packet has gone out and refuses a second one until then.

The board has its own key pair, generated on first boot and stored in flash. The private key can’t be read out, so if you want the board’s identity on the mesh you ask the board to sign and do key exchanges for you. It can also encrypt, decrypt and verify with keys you hand it. Or you skip all of that. The board sends whatever bytes you give it and doesn’t check them, so a host that keeps its own key pair builds valid packets without ever touching the board’s crypto. OpenHop does it that way. The C64 goes the other way entirely, it hasn’t got the horsepower for AES so it hands every message to the modem to encrypt or decrypt.

What it leaves out: routing, repeating, chat, room server. All of that lives on the host side.

Flashing it

Flashing is the same as any other role.

  1. Head to flasher.meshcore.io
  2. Pick your board
  3. Choose the KISS Radio Modem role
  4. Flash it
  5. Open the board’s serial port at 115200 baud, 8N1, from software that speaks MeshCore

Step 5 is where the real work lives. On nearly every board that serial port is the USB one. There is a compile-time option (KISS_UART_RX and KISS_UART_TX) to move that onto bare UART pins if you want to wire the board straight to a Pi header, but you’ll need to build the firmware yourself for that.

If you’d rather not write the serial side yourself, OpenHop already has it. If you do want to roll your own, the KISS Modem protocol doc covers the serial side and the packet format page covers what goes inside the frames.

Where to start

  • Flasher: https://flasher.meshcore.io
  • Protocol doc: https://docs.meshcore.io/kiss_modem_protocol
  • Packet format: https://docs.meshcore.io/packet_format
  • OpenHop: https://github.com/openhop-dev/openhop_repeater

If you get something running on it, post it on the Discord, I’d like to see what people wire it into.
entry.summary: What the KISS Modem firmware role is, what it isn’t, and who it’s for.

entry.title: Release v1.17.1
entry.content:
Download

Latest firmwares are in the flasher.meshcore.io

Change Log

New Features

  • #3137 new ‘get/set radio.fem.rxgain/txgain’ CLI commands (txgain is Station G3 only), fixed pref mapping for radio.fem.rxgain
  • #3148 added missing kiss radio roles, kiss radio build added to build.sh

Enhancements

  • #3106 login response no longer sent as flood on direct login, fix for unscoped flood login
  • #3146 LR2021: PREAMBLE_DETECTED bit and IRQ rx timeout logic
  • #3154 NRF52 CC310: nRFCrypto.begin()/end() now called only once
  • #3166 RadioLibWrapper noise floor debug print moved behind new MESH_DEBUG_NOISE_FLOOR flag
  • #3206 nRF RadioNoiseListener RNG now combines entropy from radio and CC310

Bug fixes and Other

  • #3140 T-Echo Lite pins aligned to updated Lilygo schematic, TCXO voltage set to 3.0V
  • #3142 build fix for R1 Neo and Minewsemi repeater
  • #3158 Rx boosted gain no longer reset to compiled value after AGC reset
  • #3164 T-Beam Supreme S3 display fix
  • #3170 ProMicro pinmap tidy up, LoRa pins moved to variant.h
  • #3185 T-Echo Card TCXO voltage set to 3.0V as per #3140
  • #3188 Heltec T096 Tx failure fixed (out of bounds PIN_SPI1_MISO)
  • #3189 Heltec T1 / MeshPocket / T-Echo Lite: unused pin fix (root cause)
  • #3203 Companion: fem_radio_rx/txgain pref disabled until settable.

Fixes and enhancements for devices with FEM

The radio.fem.rxgain setting was not being persisted properly in v1.17.0, this is now fixed. Repeater admins will want to check that radio.fem.rxgain and radio.rxgain are configured to their liking after updating. Companion firmware currently has no way to configure these settings, so they they will use the default values only for now.

Heltec T096 Transmit issue fix

The Heltec T096 transmit issue was found to be an out of bounds read of the pin map due to PIN_SPI1_MISO being set to -1. It was causing the FEM’s Tx enable pin to stop working. This has been fixed and other NRF52 boards have had their unused pins corrected.

entry.title: Release v1.17.0
entry.content:
Download

Latest firmwares are in the flasher.meshcore.io

Change Log

New Features

  • #2987 companion, MCU temperature added to sensor telemetry
  • #3115 LR2021 radio support added. (Also Meshnology W12 added)
  • #2688 new room server ‘room.post’ CLI command (for server orig posts)
  • #2883 repeater power off on long button press
  • #1727 new ‘set cad on/off’ CLI command
  • #2765 ESP targets now support the ‘get pwrmgt.bootreason’ CLI command
  • #2140 new ‘get/set radio.fem.rxgain’ CLI command (some Heltec boards)

Enhancements

  • #3036 fix for missing preamble detect IRQ bit
  • #2977 preamble and header IRQ rx timeout logic
  • #2824 nrf52 targets now use CC310 hardware crypto functions
  • #2982 config now stored in JSON format (all firmwares)
  • #3034 new color scheme on companion UI
  • #3023 room server now supports rx boosted gain
  • #2951 Fast ST7735 disply driver (Heltec T096, Wireless Tracker, etc)
  • #2895 hibernate/poweroff power draw savings

New device support

  • #3139 Sensecap X1, QSPI Flash support
  • #3122 Sensecap X1, LED and haptic feedback
  • #3112 added Sensecap MeshTracker X1 support
  • #3049 Thinknode M7 support, plus architecture for universal companion
  • #2966 added Heltec RC32 board support
  • #2560 added Heltec V4 R8 board support
  • #1983 support for RAK ethernet modules
  • #2942 added Elecrow Thinknode M9 support
  • #2839 added Elecrow Thinknode M7 support
  • #1194 added Nibble Zero Connect support
  • #2752 added Heltec tower V2 support

Bug fixes and Other

  • #3121 companion, hardware CAD disabled
  • #3107 ANON_REQ reply path_len check
  • #2863 Thinknode M6 GPS re-init fix
  • #3048 ‘start ota’ failure now reported on nRF devices
  • #2819 kiss modem fixes for stalls under USB backpressure
  • #3005 ESP32, BLE bonded reconnects fix
  • #3007 ESP32, BLE receive queue synchronization
  • #3006 Heltec V4 hardware USB serial
  • #2815 T-Beam Supreme OLED fixes
  • #2887 Thinknode M3, GPS LED fixes
  • #2990 Xiao nrf52 repeater build fix
  • #2899 T-Echo Lite DC-DC regulator fix
  • #2905 Heltec T114 DC-DC regulator fix
  • #2937 fix for GPS time sync stall on long uptime nodes
  • #2936 external watchdog timer for Heltec Tower V2
  • #2867 sx1262 LDO support fix
  • #2844 fixed rx boosted gain on LR1110
  • GPS time sync fix for Heltec T114
  • #2763 companion fix when anon contacts full
  • bad path_len now rejected, in PAYLOAD_TYPE_PATH and ANON_REQ

Packet Collision Improvements

The ‘listen-before-talk’ code has had some pretty big changes, thanks to Taco. He has spent weeks doing diagnostics, and even simulations, testing an improved scheme which involves handling cases where the LoRa radio’s IRQ flags get ‘stuck’, and also the big one being proper preamble detection. This one could be the most significant performance improvement for all meshes.

Also, he found that the new scheme performs on par with hardware CAD, but without the 4 second lock-up glitches that CAD still suffers from. So, we are still leaving hardware CAD off by default.

Companion UI

Various color displays will now sport a new look, and be much more responsive.

JSON Config

The node config should be automatically migrated to a new JSON format upon upgrading to v1.17.0. The old binary-blob config is left intact, however, in case some people need to revert to old firmware.

Steps Toward Universal Companion

With #3049 Liam has paved the way for companions to support multiple serial interfaces, eg. BLE + USB. Up to 4 can now be supported. There are no official multi-interface companion builds yet, but all the ‘plumbing’ for this is now there.

entry.title: Thank You
entry.content:
The GiveALittle fundraiser is now closed, and the results, even after the first 12 hours, were overwhelming!

We were all blown away by the response, and it has been great to know that the community has our back. There we some remarkable donations by individuals, in the thousands of dollars, but even more modest ones that were clearly by battlers not exactly well off. We also had some of the manufacturers get in touch and insisted on being anonymous donors. All of it much appreciated.

Your comments and wishes were very encouraging. Here’s a sample:

There have also been many new Github sponsor supporters, and this is equally appreciated.

Current Status

So, the UK lawyer has now officially submitted the opposition, and the trademark is now in opposed status. We don’t have any definite dates yet, but essentially it’s a waiting game now.

Hopefully there is more than enough evidence presented to determine a ruling, but the law is difficult to understand, and nothing is really guaranteed.

Onwards

The uncertainty is still difficult to deal with at times, but overall we’re positive about the future, and there are many options still available. There are solid improvements coming in the v1.17.0 release, and many more long-term improvements we are busy with. So, the tech goes on regardless.

Once again, thank you all for your generosity and your ongoing commitment to the project.

The MeshCore Team
